summary: Wind Cave National Park's 1956 steel lookout on Rankin Ridge: a 1952 crow's-nest stopgap, regular fire use until 1998, still standing but closed to climbing.

facts.design: International Derrick CL100 steel tower with 14x14 live-in cab and catwalk

access.note: Climbing the tower is not permitted. The trail to the high point is open to the public.

visit.trail_note: One-mile (1.6 km) trail through ponderosa pine to the high point, with parking at the trailhead. No pets. Climbing the historic tower is not permitted.

events.note: Planning for a lookout on the ridge began, but Emergency Conservation Work and CCC activity and then World War II stopped it.
A 40-foot cedar pole crow's nest from Elk Mountain was moved to Rankin Ridge in July as a temporary lookout.
A newspaper reported a lightning fire near Pringle spotted by the ridge lookout; three surveyors controlled it.
Permanent steel tower and cab erected by park staff, finished around September 1 at a total cost of $14,880.89.
Regular use during fire seasons ended.
Public access to the catwalk and the inside of the tower became limited.
Registered September 3, 2014 on the National Historic Lookout Register as US 1040.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The 1955 park proposal specified a 54-foot tower; firelookout.com gives 53 feet for the finished all-steel tower. The record uses the 53-foot figure from firelookout.com (16.2 m). Neither has been checked against a survey.

notes_for_editor: Strongest sources are the NPS Wind Cave assessment (npshistory.com PDF) for construction, use and 1998 access change, and the NPS trail page for current climbing rules. The 1954 newspaper quoted on westlookouts calls the Rankin Ridge watcher a State Park lookout, which does not fit the national park; the story avoids naming that person. No rental or staffing information after 1998 was found; access is recorded as closed to climbing, with the trail open. The NHLR CL100 design label and the NPS 'Standard Steel Lookout Tower' proposal are not in conflict, but only the register gives the CL100 name.
